summary.text: A Dwork–Frobenius decomposition of the exponential generating series shows that every coefficient is integral at every prime, hence the rational recursion defining the coefficients actually yields integers.  For the congruence, Wolstenholme-type bounds on reciprocal sums give the strengthened Jacobsthal estimate \(v_p(c_m(up^s)-c_m(up^{s-1}))\ge 3s+v_p(c_m(u))\); iterating the Frobenius decomposition and applying a carry-based combinatorial valuation bound forces every convolution term in the coefficient difference to have valuation at least \(3r\), with \(m=1\) reduced directly to the central-binomial case.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c_m(k):=\frac{(mk)!}{(k!)^m}\qquad (m,k\geq 0)
\]
and
\[
 D_m(x):=\sum_{k\geq1}c_m(k)x^k.
\]
Thus
\[
 A_m(x)=\exp\left(\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{c_m(k)}k x^k\right).
\]
We shall prove both that
\[
 b_m(N):=[x^N]A_m(x)^N
\]
is an integer and that, for every prime \(p\geq5\),
\[
 b_m(np^r)\equiv b_m(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}
\tag{1}
\]
whenever \(m,n,r\geq1\).

Throughout the proof, when a prime \(p\) is fixed, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation. We use the assertion
\[
 \mathcal V_k(z):\quad v_p(z)\geq k
\]
for \(z\in\mathbb Q_p\), allowing integral values of \(k\). We repeatedly use the elementary rules
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal V_k(x),\mathcal V_k(y)&\Longrightarrow \mathcal V_k(x+y),\\
 \mathcal V_k(x),\mathcal V_\ell(y)&\Longrightarrow \mathcal V_{k+\ell}(xy),\\
 \mathcal V_k(x)&\Longrightarrow \mathcal V_\ell(x)\quad(\ell\leq k),
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
and the corresponding rule for finite sums. For an integer \(z\), \(\mathcal V_k(z)\), with \(k\geq0\), is equivalent to \(p^k\mid z\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Formal exponentials
--------------------------------------------------------------------

If \(K\) is a characteristic-zero field and
\[
 D(x)=\sum_{j\geq1}d_jx^j\in K[[x]],
\]
define \(E(D)\) by the recurrence
\[
 e_0=1,\qquad
 e_k=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k d_j e_{k-j}\quad(k\geq1),
\tag{3}
\]
where \(E(D)=\sum_{k\geq0}e_kx^k\). Equivalently, \(E(D)\) is the unique series with constant term 1 satisfying
\[
 xE(D)'=D E(D).
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, comparison of the coefficient of \(x^k\) in (4) gives (3), which proves existence and uniqueness recursively. Consequently
\[
 E(D)=\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{d_j}{j}x^j\right).
\tag{5}
\]
The uniqueness in (4) also gives
\[
 E(D+D')=E(D)E(D'),\qquad E(aD)=E(D)^a
\tag{6}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(a\). If \(F(x)\mapsto F(x^q)\) is denoted by \(\operatorname{Ex}_q\), then
\[
 E(\operatorname{Ex}_qD)=\operatorname{Ex}_qE(D).
\tag{7}
\]
Finally, direct expansion of the ordinary exponential yields, for every \(N\),
\[
 [x^N]E(D)=\sum_{d=0}^N\frac1{d!}
 [x^N]\left(\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{d_j}{j}x^j\right)^d.
\tag{8}
\]
In this notation,
\[
 A_m=E(D_m),\qquad A_m^N=E(ND_m),
\tag{9}
\]
and hence
\[
 b_m(N)=[x^N]E(ND_m).
\tag{10}
\]

We shall also use the coefficient identity
\[
 c_m(k)=\prod_{a=1}^m\binom{ak}{k}.
\tag{11}
\]
It follows by successively writing
\((ak)!=\binom{ak}{k}((a-1)k)!k!\). In particular, \(c_m(k)\) is a positive integer; if \(m\geq2\), then \(\binom{2k}{k}\mid c_m(k)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A carry estimate
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a positive integer \(a\), write
\[
 a=p^{v_p(a)}a^*,\qquad p\nmid a^*.
\]
We need the following estimate. If \(m\geq2\), \(p\nmid u\), and \(u'>0\), then
\[
 v_p(u+u')\leq v_p(c_m(u))+v_p(c_m(u')).
\tag{12}
\]

To prove it, first use Kummer's description of the valuation of a binomial coefficient: \(v_p\binom{2u}{u}\) is the number of positions at which adding \(u\) to itself in base \(p\) produces a carry. Put \(k=v_p(u+u')\). For each \(1\leq i\leq k\), the congruence
\(u+u'\equiv0\pmod {p^i}\), together with \(p\nmid u\), implies
\[
 (u\bmod p^i)+(u'\bmod p^i)=p^i.
\]
Therefore at least one of the two residues is at least \(p^i/2\). Thus, at position \(i\), either adding \(u+u\) or adding \(u'+u'\) creates a carry. Counting the \(k\) positions gives
\[
 k\leq v_p\binom{2u}{u}+v_p\binom{2u'}{u'}.
\]
Now (11) and the divisibility following it imply (12).

A useful consequence, valid for nonzero \(a,b\), is
\[
 v_p(a+b)\leq v_p(a)+v_p(b)
   +v_p(c_m(a^*))+v_p(c_m(b^*)).
\tag{13}
\]
If \(v_p(a)\neq v_p(b)\), the valuation of the sum is the smaller valuation, so (13) is immediate. If both valuations equal \(s\), then
\[
 v_p(a+b)=s+v_p(a^*+b^*),
\]
and (13) follows from (12).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Wolstenholme sums and the strong Jacobsthal estimate
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(M\geq1\), let
\[
 I_p(M)=\{1\leq i<M:p\nmid i\}.
\]
(The omission or inclusion of the endpoint makes no difference below when \(p\mid M\), since the endpoint is then divisible by \(p\).)

Suppose \(p\geq5\), \(u\geq1\), and \(p^u\mid M\). We claim
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_{i\in I_p(M)}\frac1{i^2}\right)\geq u,
\tag{14}
\]
and
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_{i\in I_p(M)}\frac1i\right)\geq2u.
\tag{15}
\]

For (14), first take \(M=q=p^u\). Multiplication by 2 permutes the nonzero residue classes modulo \(q\) which are prime to \(p\). If
\[
 T=\sum_{i\in I_p(q)}i^{-2},
\]
then replacing \(i\) by \(2i\bmod q\) changes each inverse square, modulo \(p^u\), to \((2i)^{-2}\). Hence
\[
 T\equiv \frac14T\pmod {p^u}.
\]
Since 3 and 4 are \(p\)-adic units, \(T\equiv0\pmod {p^u}\). If \(M=kq\), divide the range into blocks \(jq+i\). For each \(i\) prime to \(p\),
\[
 (jq+i)^{-2}\equiv i^{-2}\pmod {p^u},
\]
so summing the block congruences proves (14).

For (15), pair \(i\) with \(M-i\). Both are prime to \(p\), and
\[
 \frac1i+\frac1{M-i}
 =M\left(-\frac1{i^2}+M\frac1{i^2(M-i)}\right).
\tag{16}
\]
After summation, the first term on the right has valuation at least \(u+u=2u\) by (14), while the second has valuation at least \(2u\), since all denominators are \(p\)-adic units. The left side of the summed identity is twice \(\sum i^{-1}\); as 2 is a unit, (15) follows.

We now derive the needed Jacobsthal congruence. Splitting factorials into factors divisible and not divisible by \(p\) gives the exact identity
\[
 \binom{(K+D)p}{Kp}\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}i
 =\binom{K+D}{K}\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}(i+Dp).
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, in \((Kp)!\) the divisible factors contribute \(p^K K!\), and the remaining factors give the first product; applying the same split to the rising factorial \((Dp+1)\cdots(Dp+Kp)\) gives (17).

Assume \(s\geq1\), \(p^{s-1}\mid K\), and \(p^{s-1}\mid D\). Put
\[
 Y=\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}i,
 \qquad X=\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}(i+Dp).

data
\]
Then
\[
 \frac XY=\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}\left(1+\frac{Dp}{i}\right).
\tag{18}
\]
Every \(Dp/i\) has valuation at least \(s\). Expanding a product through degree two,
\[
 \prod_i(1+x_i)=1+\sum_i x_i+
 \frac{(\sum_i x_i)^2-\sum_i x_i^2}{2}+R,
\tag{19}
\]
where every term of \(R\) has degree at least three and therefore valuation at least \(3s\). By (15), applied with \(M=Kp\),
\[
 v_p\left(Dp\sum_i i^{-1}\right)\geq s+2s=3s.
\]
By (14),
\[
 v_p\left((Dp)^2\sum_i i^{-2}\right)\geq2s+s=3s.
\]
The square of the first sum has still larger valuation. Thus (19) gives
\[
 \frac XY\equiv1\pmod {p^{3s}}.
\tag{20}
\]
This is the strong Jacobsthal estimate. Without (14) and (15), the elementary fact that each factor in (18) is \(1\pmod {p^s}\) gives the weaker estimate modulo \(p^s\), which will also be used.

Apply (17) successively to the product (11). One obtains the exact identity
\[
 c_m(Kp)=c_m(K)\prod_{a=0}^{m-1}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}(i+aKp)}
      {\prod_{i\in I_p(Kp)}i}.
\tag{21}
\]
Every quotient in (21) has \(p\)-adic norm 1. Therefore
\[
 v_p(c_m(Kp))=v_p(c_m(K)),
\tag{22}
\]
and iteration gives
\[
 v_p(c_m(up^t))=v_p(c_m(u)).
\tag{23}
\]
Using (20) in (21), and noting that multiplication by \(c_m(K)\) adds \(v_p(c_m(K))\) to the valuation, gives
\[
 v_p(c_m(Kp)-c_m(K))
 \geq3s+v_p(c_m(K))
\tag{24}
\]
whenever \(p^{s-1}\mid K\). Hence, for \(s\geq1\),
\[
 v_p\bigl(c_m(up^s)-c_m(up^{s-1})\bigr)
 \geq3s+v_p(c_m(u)).
\tag{25}
\]
The weak version of the same argument is
\[
 v_p\bigl(c_m(up^s)-c_m(up^{s-1})\bigr)\geq s.
\tag{26}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Integrality of the exponential coefficients
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix an arbitrary prime \(p\). Define
\[
 \Delta_m(x):=pD_m(x)-pD_m(x^p).
\tag{27}
\]
The coefficient of \(x^i\) in its formal integral
\[
 J_m(x):=\sum_{i\geq1}\frac{[x^i]\Delta_m}{i}x^i
\]
has valuation at least 1. To see this, write \(i=up^s\), \(p\nmid u\). If \(s=0\), that coefficient is \(pc_m(i)/i\), which is divisible by \(p\). If \(s>0\), it is
\[
 \frac p i\left(c_m(up^s)-c_m(up^{s-1})\right),
\]
and (26) gives valuation at least \(1+s-s=1\).

It follows from the exponential expansion (8) that every nonconstant coefficient of \(E(\Delta_m)\) is divisible by \(p\). Indeed, the term involving \(J_m^d/d!\) has valuation at least
\(d-v_p(d!)\geq1\) for \(d>0\).

From (6), (7), and (27), we have the fundamental one-step identity
\[
 E(NpD_m)=E(NpD_m(x^p))E(N\Delta_m)
 =E(ND_m)(x^p)E(N\Delta_m).
\tag{28}
\]
We now prove that every coefficient of \(E(D_m)\) is \(p\)-integral. Let
\(F=E(D_m)\), and argue by strong induction on the coefficient index \(i\). The constant coefficient is 1. Assume all coefficients below \(i>0\) are integral, and let
\[
 T(x)=\sum_{j<i}[x^j]F\,x^j.
\]
The induction hypothesis makes all coefficients of \(T\) integral. Fermat's congruence in the residue field gives
\[
 T(x)^p\equiv T(x^p)\pmod p
\tag{29}
\]
coefficientwise: for a monomial this is \(a^p\equiv a\pmod p\), and the mixed terms in a \(p\)-th power have binomial coefficients divisible by \(p\).

On the other hand, (28) with \(N=1\), together with \(E(pD_m)=F^p\), says
\[
 F^p=F(x^p)E(\Delta_m).
\tag{30}
\]
Since all nonconstant coefficients of the second factor are divisible by \(p\), comparison of the coefficient of \(x^i\), using the induction hypothesis on the coefficients of \(F(x^p)\) which occur in the nonconstant convolution terms, gives
\[
 [x^i]F^p-[x^i]F(x^p)\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{31}
\]
Because \(F-T\) begins with \(([x^i]F)x^i\), while both \(F\) and \(T\) have constant term 1, the difference-of-powers identity gives
\[
 [x^i](F^p-T^p)=p[x^i]F.
\tag{32}
\]
Moreover \([x^i]F(x^p)=[x^i]T(x^p)\): if \(p\mid i\), this compares the coefficient at \(i/p<i\), and otherwise both sides are zero. Combining (29), (31), and (32) shows that \(p[x^i]F\) has valuation at least 1, hence \([x^i]F\) is integral. This completes the induction.

By (6), all coefficients of
\[
 E(ND_m)=E(D_m)^N
\tag{33}
\]
are \(p\)-integral for every prime \(p\). They are rational numbers, and a rational number integral at every prime has denominator 1: if a prime divided its reduced denominator, its valuation at that prime would be negative. Thus all coefficients in (33), in particular \(b_m(N)\), are integers.

This also justifies the elementary integer recurrence used to calculate them. If \(d_j=Nc_m(j)\), then (3) says
\[
 e_0=1,\qquad e_k=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k d_j e_{k-j}.
\tag{34}
\]
The preceding argument proves that each quotient is an integer. Since all summands are nonnegative, the coefficients are nonnegative integers, and (34) is exactly the recursively defined integer sequence associated with \(A_m(x)^N\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A refined bound for the correction exponential
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now again fix \(p\geq5\), and assume \(m\geq2\). For \(i>0\), put
\[
 v=v_p(i),\qquad i^*=i/p^v,
 \qquad \beta(i^*)=v_p(c_m(i^*)).
\]
Using the strong estimate (25) instead of (26) in the preceding calculation gives
\[
 v_p([x^i]J_m)\geq1+2v+\beta(i^*).
\tag{35}
\]
Indeed, if \(v=0\), the coefficient is \(pc_m(i)/i\), giving \(1+\beta(i)\). If \(v>0\), (25) gives valuation at least
\[
 1-v+(3v+\beta(i^*))=1+2v+\beta(i^*).
\]

Suppose \(p^\kappa\mid N\), and define
\[
 \Psi(\kappa,\beta,v)
 =1+\kappa+2\min(v,\kappa+1)
   +\max\bigl(0,\min(\beta,\kappa+1-v)\bigr).
\tag{36}
\]
We claim that, for \(i>0\),
\[
 v_p\bigl([x^i]E(N\Delta_m)\bigr)
 \geq \Psi\bigl(\kappa,\beta(i^*),v_p(i)\bigr).
\tag{37}
\]

By (8), the coefficient in question is a sum of the coefficients of
\((NJ_m)^d/d!\). We estimate separately:

* For \(d=0\), the coefficient is zero because \(i>0\).

* For \(d=1\), (35) plus \(v_p(N)\geq\kappa\) gives the desired result directly from (36).

* For \(d=2\), write \(i=a+b\), with \(a,b>0\); terms with \(a=0\) or \(b=0\) vanish because \(J_m(0)=0\). The valuation supplied by (35) to the product indexed by \((a,b)\), together with the factor \(N^2/2\), is
\[
 2\kappa+2+2v_p(a)+2v_p(b)
 +v_p(c_m(a^*))+v_p(c_m(b^*)).
\]
Since 2 is a \(p\)-adic unit, there is no loss from division by 2. Inequality (13), with \(a+b=i\), shows that this is at least the right side of (37). This is precisely the reason for the last, truncated \(\beta\)-term in (36).

* For \(d\geq3\), the weaker consequence \(v_p([x^j]J_m)\geq1\) gives
\[
 v_p\left([x^i]\frac{(NJ_m)^d}{d!}\right)
 \geq d\kappa+d-v_p(d!).
\tag{38}
\]
For \(p\geq5\), Legendre's formula implies
\[
 4v_p(d!)+1\leq d.
\tag{39}
\]
Also, directly from (36),
\[
 \Psi(\kappa,\beta,v)\leq3(\kappa+1).
\tag{40}
\]
For \(d\geq3\), (39) implies that the lower bound in (38) is at least (40), and hence at least \(\Psi\).

Thus every summand has the required valuation, proving (37).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Iterating the one-step decomposition
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(\operatorname{Ex}_tF:=F(x^{p^t})\). Iterating (28) gives
\[
 E(np^rD_m)=
 \operatorname{Ex}_r E(nD_m)
 \prod_{t=0}^{r-1}
 \operatorname{Ex}_t E(np^{r-1-t}\Delta_m).
\tag{41}
\]
Using (28) once more at the final step, we can express the coefficient difference in (1) as one coefficient of a product. Define factors indexed by \(0\leq t\leq r\):
\[
 G_0=E(np^{r-1}\Delta_m)-1,
\]
\[
 G_t=\operatorname{Ex}_tE(np^{r-1-t}\Delta_m)
 \quad(0<t<r),
\]
and
\[
 G_r=\operatorname{Ex}_rE(nD_m).
\]
Then (41) and (28) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &[x^{np^r}]E(np^rD_m)-[x^{np^{r-1}}]E(np^{r-1}D_m)\\
 &\hspace{35mm}=[x^{np^r}]\prod_{t=0}^rG_t.
\end{aligned}
\tag{42}
\]
The second coefficient on the left appears because
\([x^{Np}]F(x^p)=[x^N]F(x)\).

For bookkeeping, define, for \(x>0\),
\[
 \psi_t(x)=r+2\min(v_p(x),r)-3t
 +\max\bigl(0,\min(\beta(x^*),r-v_p(x))\bigr),
\tag{43}
\]
where \(\beta(u)=v_p(c_m(u))\). The refined estimate (37), after accounting for the substitution \(x\mapsto x^{p^t}\), gives the following bounds.

* For \(t=0\), the constant coefficient of \(G_0\) is zero, and for \(x>0\),
\[
 v_p([x^x]G_0)\geq\psi_0(x).
\]

* For \(0<t<r\), the constant coefficient of \(G_t\) is 1. If \(p^t\nmid x\), the coefficient is zero; if \(x>0\) and \(p^t\mid x\), then
\[
 v_p([x^x]G_t)\geq\psi_t(x).
\]

* For \(t=r\), all coefficients are integral by Section 4, and a coefficient vanishes unless \(p^r\mid x\).

For uniformity, assign valuation bound \(3r\) whenever one of the stated divisibility conditions fails, since the corresponding coefficient is zero; assign bound \(3r\) to the zero coefficient of \(G_0\); and assign bound zero to the permitted coefficients of \(G_r\) and to the constant coefficients of the middle factors. Call this uniform bound \(\phi_t(x)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. The combinatorial valuation lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove that whenever nonnegative integers \(l_0,\ldots,l_r\) satisfy
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^r l_t=np^r,
\tag{44}
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^r\phi_t(l_t)\geq3r.
\tag{45}
\]

If \(l_0=0\), its assigned bound is already \(3r\). If for some \(0<t<r\), \(l_t>0\) but \(p^t\nmid l_t\), that factor alone has bound \(3r\). The same is true if \(p^r\nmid l_r\). We may therefore assume
\[
 l_0>0,\qquad p^t\mid l_t\text{ whenever }0<t<r\text{ and }l_t>0,
 \qquad p^r\mid l_r.
\tag{46}
\]
Let
\[
 S=\{t<r:l_t>0\}.
\]
Then \(0\in S\), \(p^t\mid l_t\) for \(t\in S\), and, by subtracting \(l_r\) from (44),
\[
 p^r\mid\sum_{t\in S}l_t.
\tag{47}
\]
On this set \(\phi_t(l_t)=\psi_t(l_t)\), and every \(\psi_t(l_t)\) is nonnegative because \(t\leq v_p(l_t)\) and \(t<r\). It remains to prove
\[
 \sum_{t\in S}\psi_t(l_t)\geq3r.
\tag{48}
\]

Let
\[
 s=\min_{t\in S}v_p(l_t).
\]
If \(s\geq r\), then \(v_p(l_0)\geq r\), and (43) gives
\(\psi_0(l_0)\geq3r\), proving (48).

Assume henceforth \(s<r\). Divisibility (47) implies that the minimum valuation \(s\) occurs at least twice. Otherwise, after removing its unique occurrence, the remaining sum would be divisible by \(p^{s+1}\), forcing the exceptional term also to be divisible by \(p^{s+1}\), a contradiction.

For every term of valuation exactly \(s\), formula (43), together with \(t\leq s\), gives
\[
 \psi_t(l_t)\geq r-s.
\tag{49}
\]
We now distinguish the necessary cases.

First suppose \(v_p(l_0)>s\). Then there are two other indices of valuation \(s\). Since \(v_p(l_0)\geq s+1\),
\[
 \psi_0(l_0)\geq r+2(s+1).
\]
Adding the two bounds (49) gives at least
\[
 r+2s+2+2(r-s)>3r.
\]

We may therefore suppose \(v_p(l_0)=s\). Choose \(t\neq0\) with \(v_p(l_t)=s\). Then
\[
 \psi_0(l_0)\geq r+2s,
 \qquad \psi_t(l_t)\geq r-s.
\tag{50}
\]
If there is a third index, distinct from 0 and \(t\), also of valuation \(s\), another application of (49) proves (48).

It remains to treat the case in which 0 and \(t\) are the only indices of valuation \(s\). Write
\[
 l_0=p^su,
 \qquad l_t=p^su',
 \qquad p\nmid uu'.

data
\]
Put \(s'=v_p(u+u')\). The other terms are all divisible by \(p^{s+1}\), and the total sum is divisible by \(p^r\), so \(s'\geq1\). By the carry estimate (12),
\[
 s'\leq\beta(u)+\beta(u').
\tag{51}
\]
The last terms in (43), together with (51), sharpen (50) to the combined estimate
\[
 \psi_0(l_0)+\psi_t(l_t)
 \geq 2r+4s-3t+\min(s',r-s).
\tag{52}
\]
Also \(t\leq s\), because \(p^t\mid l_t\).

If \(s+s'\geq r\), (52) immediately gives at least \(3r\). If \(s+s'<r\), there must be some third index \(t''\), distinct from 0 and \(t\), with
\[
 v_p(l_{t''})\leq s+s'.
\tag{53}
\]
For otherwise all remaining terms would be divisible by \(p^{s+s'+1}\); (47) would force \(l_0+l_t=p^s(u+u')\) to have that divisibility as well, contradicting the definition of \(s'\). From (43), (53), and \(t''\leq v_p(l_{t''})\), one gets
\[
 \psi_{t''}(l_{t''})\geq r-s-s'.
\tag{54}
\]
Adding (52) and (54), using \(t\leq s\), again gives at least \(3r\). This proves (48), and hence (45), in every case.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Completion for \(m\geq2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Expand the coefficient on the right of (42) by convolution. Each term is indexed by a tuple \((l_0,\ldots,l_r)\) satisfying (44), and equals
\[
 \prod_{t=0}^r[x^{l_t}]G_t.
\]
The coefficient bounds of Section 6 and the multiplicative valuation rule (2) show that its valuation is at least
\(\sum_t\phi_t(l_t)\), which is at least \(3r\) by (45). The ultrametric inequality then gives the same lower bound for the sum of all convolution terms. Thus
\[
 v_p\left(b_m(np^r)-b_m(np^{r-1})\right)\geq3r

data
\]
for \(m\geq2\). Since both quantities are integers, this is precisely congruence (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. The case \(m=1\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Here \(c_1(k)=1\), and therefore
\[
 A_1(x)=\exp\left(\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{x^k}{k}\right)
 =(1-x)^{-1}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 b_1(N)=[x^N](1-x)^{-N}=\binom{2N-1}{N}
 =\frac12\binom{2N}{N}=\frac12c_2(N).
\tag{55}
\]
Apply (25) with \(m=2\), \(u=n\), and \(s=r\). It gives
\[
 v_p(c_2(np^r)-c_2(np^{r-1}))
 \geq3r+v_p(c_2(n))\geq3r.
\]
Because \(p\geq5\), division by 2 does not change the \(p\)-adic valuation. Equation (55) therefore proves (1) for \(m=1\) as well.

Combining Sections 4, 8, and 9 proves that for every positive integer \(m\), all coefficients \(b_m(N)=[x^N]A_m(x)^N\) are integers and, for every prime \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
 \boxed{\ b_m(np^r)\equiv b_m(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}\ }.
\]
